title: 5.13.5 Lab: Steer it
description: The block only walks right and walks off the edge. Add the four arrow keys with two direction variables, forbid turning back on yourself, and end the round at a wall.

steps.title: Turn with the arrow keys
steps.instructions: The block moves by `dx` and `dy` each step, but nothing changes them. In `draw()`, set `dx` and `dy` when an arrow key is pressed: up is `dx = 0; dy = -1`, and so on for down, left and right.
hints: `kb.presses('up')` is true on the frame the key goes down.
Four `if` lines, one per key. Each sets both `dx` and `dy` so the block never moves diagonally.

steps.title: No turning back
steps.instructions: Pressing the opposite key while moving would send the snake straight back into itself. Allow up and down only when `dy === 0`, and left and right only when `dx === 0`.
hints: Add `&& dy === 0` to the up and down tests, and `&& dx === 0` to left and right.
Run it and press left while moving right. Nothing should happen.

steps.title: Stop at the wall
steps.instructions: After the step, if the new column or row is off the grid (below 0, or 20 or more), set `playing` to `false`. Otherwise move the block on screen: the two pixel lines already in the starter go in the `else`, so a dead block stays on the last cell it reached. The starter already shows 'Game over' when `playing` is false, from `drawTop()` at the bottom, so the block can never cover the words.
hints: `if (...off the grid...) { playing = false; } else { head.x = ...; head.y = ...; }`

requirements.title: Each arrow key sets the direction
requirements.description: Pressing up, down, left or right changes dx and dy together. Help: 5.13.2 (Reading: A world on a grid)

requirements.title: A turn straight back is refused
requirements.description: Each of the four keys refuses a turn straight back: up and down only when the block is not already moving up or down (dy === 0), left and right only when dx === 0. Help: 5.13.2 (Reading: A world on a grid)

requirements.title: Leaving the grid ends the round
requirements.description: A column or row off the grid sets the flag false. Help: 5.12.3 (Lab: Crash, and start again)

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote a moSHion sketch (p5-style JavaScript with a physics world) for the lab "5.13.5 Lab: Steer it". The task they were given: The block (head) moves one cell per beat by dx and dy on a 20 by 20 grid of 20-pixel cells. In draw(), set dx and dy when an arrow key is pressed: up is dx = 0, dy = -1, and so on for down, left and right, each key setting both. Refuse a turn straight back: allow up and down only when dy === 0, and left and right only when dx === 0. After the step, if the new column or row is off the grid (below 0, or 20 or more), set playing to false; otherwise move the block on screen. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do when the sketch runs. y grows DOWNWARD, so up is a negative row change. kb.presses('up') is true on the frame the key goes down and kb.pressing('up') on every frame it is held; the arrow keys and w/a/s/d answer to the same names 'up', 'down', 'left' and 'right'. head.col and head.row are the block's cell (0 to 19), and cellToPixel turns a cell number into pixels. The starter already shows 'Game over' when playing is false. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, template strings, arrow functions, ternaries or if-chains, semicolons, spacing, quotes, order and helper functions of their own are all fine; only a name the starter's own code already calls or reads has to keep that name. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment or a string never runs, so the starter's STEP comments are never the student's work. A key that sets only one of dx and dy leaves the other at its old value, so the block can move diagonally. So for the arrow-key criterion, read the lines under EACH of the four key tests one by one and list what each sets: every key must set both dx and dy, one of them to 0. If even one key sets only dy (or only dx), that criterion is partial, not met, even when the other keys set both; do not say a key sets both values unless you can point to both assignments under it. Up with dy = 1 (or down with dy = -1) is the opposite direction. For the turn-back rule, dy === 0, dy == 0, !dy, or ruling out only the straight-back case (up refused while dy is 1, written dy !== 1) all do the job, written with && or as an if inside an if, in either order. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise. Write for a 14-year-old beginner: short sentences and everyday words.

rubric.title: Each arrow key sets the direction
rubric.description: Four key tests (up, down, left, right; presses or pressing), each setting BOTH dx and dy for the direction it names: up dx = 0 and dy = -1, down dx = 0 and dy = 1, left dx = -1 and dy = 0, right dx = 1 and dy = 0. Check the code under each of the four keys on its own: up and down must also set dx to 0, and left and right must also set dy to 0. Separate ifs, else if or a switch are all fine. Partial: a key is missing, or any one key sets only one of dx and dy (the other keeps its old value, so the block moves diagonally). Missing: no key changes the direction, or the directions are reversed. Help: 5.13.2 (Reading: A world on a grid)

rubric.title: A turn straight back is refused
rubric.description: Each of the four key tests also checks the current direction so the block cannot turn back onto itself: up and down only when it is not already moving up or down (dy === 0, or the straight-back case ruled out with dy !== 1 for up and dy !== -1 for down), left and right only when dx === 0 (or the matching !== test). Partial: some keys are guarded and some are not. Missing: no key checks the direction. Help: 5.13.2 (Reading: A world on a grid)

rubric.title: Leaving the grid ends the round
rubric.description: After the step, a test of the new column or row being off the grid (below 0, or 20 or more; > 19 and === -1 style tests also count) sets playing to false. Testing all four sides is what step 3 asks; a test that clearly covers leaving the grid counts here. Moving the block on screen only in the else is also what step 3 asks and is welcome. Missing: nothing sets playing to false, or it is set false while the block is still on the grid. Help: 5.12.3 (Lab: Crash, and start again)
